subject: Model comparison favours different models for hierarchical and non-hierarchical set-up?

messages.author: 90b5ae7e2259370d
messages.subject: Model comparison favours different models for hierarchical and non-hierarchical set-up?
parts:
Dear all,

I  have a problem understanding discrepancies between different model comparison results for a hierarchical vs. non-hierarchical instantiation of the same model and I can't think of what could have caused the problem.

I've got two models (for a reinforcement learning task in humans) that, when I fit my 30 participants individually, e.g. using matlab's fminsearch, I find that model A is vastly better than B (BIC difference is ~200, for the BIC summed across all participants). When I fit people individually in Stan, I see similarly that the log likelihood for each person massively favours model A.

But, when I use a hierarchical model in Stan, model B is strongly favoured. This is both the case when I do a leave-one participant-out cross validation (i.e. getting the log likelihood for the left out participant, by drawing his parameters randomly using the group priors in the generated quantities block) or when I fit all participants together hierarchically and just look at their log likelihoods.

As an aside, when I compare parameters for people either generated by a hierarchical or an independent model, they correlate strongly (r is ~0.8-0.9).

I am not sure whether this model fit result is even possible or whether it means that I must have made a coding error somewhere?? 

The only other thing that I have come up with so far is that maybe it's a problem with the parameters not being normally distributed on the group level? (though i am not sure whether this could even explain the model fit discrepancy). For many of the parameters I assume that they are normally distributed on one scale (e.g. from - to + infinity) and then I transform them to another scale (e.g. from 0 to 1). I've attached a figure that shows in the top row all the parameters from individual participants after i've adjusted them and the bottom row is the parameters before i've adjusted them. It looks like maybe there is a problem for 'lrnw' (which means 'how much you weight what you have learnt when you make a decision'). I'm sampling this as lrnw and then transform it so that lrnw_adj=1/(1+lrnw). And I'm assuming that lrnw is normally distributed, but this is clearly not true.

I would be very grateful for any advice
Jacquie

messages.author: 90b5ae7e2259370d
messages.subject: Re: Model comparison favours different models for hierarchical and non-hierarchical set-up?
parts: so yes, turns out that if I put a hierarchical prior on a parameterisation of the parameter that is normally distributed (based on having fitted individual participants separately), the log likelihoods look much more like what I would have expected.

messages.author: 90b5ae7e2259370d
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Model comparison favours different models for hierarchical and non-hierarchical set-up?
parts:
Hi Daniel,

kind of - using new priors means now that model 1 has better log likelihoods for the fitted participants, but in terms of log likelihoods for the left out participant, model 4 is still better. Now of course that could mean that model 4 is the better model; but I would be surprised because if I fit each participant individually the BIC massively favours model 1 (and some other analyses do as well). I've attached a screenshot of how the model fits looks; the column of numbers are the log likelihoods for the 26 participants I used to fit the model (StanAll.n26loglik) and the number at the bottom is the leave-one out log likelihood for the remaining participant (StanAll.loologlik)

I've attached the scripts. I'm sorry the model is quite long. It's a basic reinforcement learner where people learn about reward magnitudes and probabilities and effort magnitudes. The two models just differ in how they compute the value of the two options that the participants compare and choose between:
it's either 
util <- relRe*lrnW*rmp[t,o]+ (1-lrnW)*prob[is,t,o] - (1-relRE)*lrnW*emp[t,o]    {M1}
which means:
utility of an option is the weighted some of reward magnitude (rmp), probability (prob) and effort magnitude (emp).

and in model 4 it is:
util <- (1-effW)*rmp[t,o]*prob[is,t,o]/100 - effW*emp[t,o]    {M4}
so here reward magnitude and probability are multiplied together.

I'm not sure whether the error could be anything to do with how I draw parameters in the generated quantities block?
I use the normal_rng and then transform the parameters as in the model.

I would be very grateful for advice on this
Jacquie

just to add - i've done some data simulation now using e.g. model 1 and it turns out that even with simulated data the leave-one out log likelihoods are not correct (i.e. even when I simulate data from model 1, the loo prefers model 4 for some samples). Even though the log likelihoods for the participants that I'm using to fit the model (i.e. n-1 = 29) do consistently favour the model I used to create the data. 

I wonder whether the problem is because the model is hierarchical and I'm leaving out 1 out of 30 people each time? I am not sure what checks I could be doing on my modelling results to track down the problem?

parts:

> just to add - i've done some data simulation now using e.g. model 1 and it turns out that even with simulated data the leave-one out log likelihoods are not correct (i.e. even when I simulate data from model 1, the loo prefers model 4 for some samples). Even though the log likelihoods for the participants that I'm using to fit the model (i.e. n-1 = 29) do consistently favour the model I used to create the data.
>
> I wonder whether the problem is because the model is hierarchical and I'm leaving out 1 out of 30 people each time? I am not sure what checks I could be doing on my modelling results to track down the problem?

If the log likelihoods are not correct, then that seems like
the biggest clue to help track down where the problem is. Is it
that if you give it data it gives you the wrong log density or
are parameter estimates off?

I'd suggest taking the simulated data from model 1 and making
sure that 50% of the parameters are estimated in their
posterior 50% intervals and if not, trying to jointly debug
the simulation and Stan program code until they match.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Model comparison favours different models for hierarchical and non-hierarchical set-up?
parts:
I've found a possible solution: I've noticed that some parameters that are fitted are correlated. However, when I generate new parameters for the left out participant (in generated quantities block) they will not be correlated. I was wondering whether this might be an explanation why log likelihoods for the fitted participants are as expected (and parameters are recovered well by the model for simulated data) but log likelihoods for the left out participants are not as expected?


To address this, I've thought of two possibilities, I've tried one now, I've fitted my model on half the data from each participant (which in my case made sense because the data was collected in two independent sessions for each person). I use the parameter estimates from that to then compute the log likelihoods for the second half of the data set. This shows the pattern that I would predict.


The second solution which I have not tried yet (and I'm not sure whether it would be better) is a leave-one-out cross validation in several steps: 1) Fit models to data of n-1 participants to get estimates of mean and standard deviations for hyper parameters. 2) Use these to simulate say 1000 new participants (they will have uncorrelated parameters). 3) Fit the data of these 1000 new participants with the model. This will give me somewhat correlated parameter estimates. 4) Use these 1000 estimated parameter sets to compute the log likelihood for the left out participant [the main advantage now is that I will have realistic parameter sets with some correlations between parameters]. Repeat all steps, leaving out a different participant each time. I am not sure whether this method has any advantage over what I've done now? (I guess it would answer my question whether the problem was that I'm not capturing correlations between parameters?)


--> My main question is now whether in general a leave-one-out cross validation for hierarchical models (leaving out participants rather than trials within participants) is problematic when parameters are somewhat correlated?

parts:
Parameters are correlated by design in a hierarchical model.
That's where the partial pooling comes from.

Also, see Wei and Andrew's paper on the topic:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/final_sub.pdf

I believe the loo package in R will do this for you.
Aki, Andrew, and Jonah have a new paper on this topic, too:

http://andrewgelman.com/2016/10/21/practical-loo/

-Bob

parts:
Hi Jacquie,

Based on your description my guess is that there is large variation between subjects and thus the inferred population distributions (priors) are wide. In that case it is really difficult to predict well the observations for left-out-subject. The correlation issue you mention hints that instead of independent population distributions you currently use, you might need a joint population distribution for the correlating variables to model the correlations.

Aki
